opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, Yann was a big part of it. When I was deciding where to go after industry, I wasn't just looking for a job title. I was looking for a place where the research culture matched what I cared about. Yann has always been someone who thinks about the long-term questions in AI: how machines can learn about the world the way humans and animals do, mostly through observation, without massive amounts of labels. That's very close to what I've been obsessed with in my own work on representation learning and visual understanding.

Having him there sends a signal. It tells you the place is serious about fundamental research, not just chasing the next benchmark. He's also very independent in his thinking. He's willing to say things that go against the mainstream, like his skepticism that scaling language models alone will get us to real intelligence. Whether or not you agree with every point, being around someone like that keeps you honest. It pushes you to ask whether you're working on something that actually matters.

There's also a practical side. NYU, partly because of Yann, has built a strong community around deep learning and computer vision, and it attracts very good students who want to work on ambitious, open-ended problems. For a young faculty member, that ecosystem matters a lot. You can collaborate, you can argue about ideas, and your students benefit from that environment too.

So it wasn't only "I want to work with a Turing Award winner." It was more that his presence shaped a kind of intellectual home, one that values vision, in both senses of the word, and that felt like the right place for me to build my own lab.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it mattered a lot, maybe more than any single factor. When I was deciding where to go after my time in industry, I was thinking about what kind of environment I wanted to do research in for the next decade. And Yann being at NYU meant a few concrete things.

First, there's the obvious one: he's one of the people who basically built the field I work in. Convolutional networks, the whole idea that you should learn representations from data rather than hand-design them. I grew up academically on that work. So having him down the hall, being able to just walk over and argue about something, that's not something you can replicate elsewhere.

But the second thing is more subtle, and I think it's actually the bigger reason. Yann has very strong, sometimes contrarian opinions about where AI should go. He's been skeptical of a lot of the mainstream directions, he pushes self-supervised learning, world models, this idea that scaling language models alone won't get us there. And whether or not you agree with every one of those positions, it creates an intellectual culture where you're allowed to disagree with the consensus. For someone like me, who likes to work on things that are a bit off the beaten path, that's a very valuable thing. At NYU you're not punished for betting against the trend.

The third thing is more practical. His presence attracts a certain kind of student and a certain kind of collaborator. People who come to NYU for AI often come because they care about fundamental questions, not just chasing the next benchmark. And as a new faculty member, your students are everything. The quality and taste of the people around you shapes what you end up doing.

I'd also say, and this is something I didn't fully appreciate until I got there, that Yann is very generous with junior faculty. He doesn't try to make everyone work on his agenda. He'll tell you what he thinks, often very directly, but then he lets you go do your own thing. That combination of a strong point of view and genuine openness is rare, and it's part of why I felt NYU was the right place for me.
